title: Sombrero Galaxy (NIRCam)
caption: The Sombrero Galaxy (M104) in near-infrared light, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
celestial: Sombrero Galaxy, M104 · constellation Virgo · about About 30 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: NASA Webb image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: A long, brownish-yellow disk tilts across the frame from upper left to lower right, its rim edged with mottled dark brown patches. This is the Sombrero Galaxy, also called M104, in near-infrared light from the NIRCam instrument on the James Webb Space Telescope. It lies around 30 million light-years away, on the fringe of the Virgo galaxy cluster, and we see it nearly edge-on.

Dust in the outer ring blocks some light from stars inside the galaxy, but less than in Hubble's visible-light view, because longer infrared wavelengths slip past dust more easily. The huge central bulge of packed stars shines through, along with roughly 2,000 globular clusters, dense balls each holding hundreds of thousands of old stars.

The clusters hint at a turbulent past, since their stars differ chemically from one another, which a merger of galaxies over billions of years would explain. Our viewpoint sits six degrees off the galaxy's equator, and from there the inner disk looks tilted inward like the start of a funnel, a warp that also supports the merger idea.
scale: NASA lists this view as about 6.0 arcminutes across, roughly 52,000 light-years at the object’s distance.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam took this near-infrared image. NASA shows the F090W and F200W filters in blue, F212N and F277W in green, and F335M and F444W in red.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and at these wavelengths the dark dust lane that dominates visible-light views is much less pronounced.

explore: The Sombrero has a mass of about 800 billion Suns. NIRCam also picks out individual red giant stars outside the galaxy, though not necessarily at its distance. These cool stars glow brightly because of their large surface area. Background galaxies of many shapes and colours fill the rest of the field, and their colours give astronomers clues to properties such as their distance.
